item.title: 11/2/26 – Prep: Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office, Georgia
item.description: In April 2019 Fulton County District Attorney Paul Howard hired Jasmine Younge as his Deputy Chief of Staff and Director of Policy and Programs, the third-ranking job in the office. She supervised more than thirty employees, reported only to Howard and testified that she was his "go-to person for almost everything." On about July 1 she told Howard she was pregnant. She alleges that he reacted angrily, cut her out of meetings and reassigned her duties, and he fired her on July 15. Howard testified that he had already told her she was not working out; his chief of staff testified she knew of no discussion of firing Younge before the announcement. The office answered Younge's Title Seven suit, N.D. Ga.; her other claims were dismissed or abandoned, on March 24, 2021. The answer listed several affirmative defenses but not the section 2000e f personal-staff exemption, although it admitted she was a member of the DA's "executive and/or personal staff." The scheduling order's deadline to amend pleadings passed on May 26, 2021, and discovery closed January 5, 2022. At a March 14, 2022 discovery hearing the office first said it would rely on the exemption; counsel said he had not realized it was an issue until he began drafting the summary judgment motion. On May 16, 2022 it moved for summary judgment on that exemption and on the separate "policymaking appointee" exemption, without ever seeking leave to amend. Applying Hassan versus U.S. Postal Service, the magistrate judge treated the exemption as an affirmative defense and found it had not been pleaded or noticed before March 2022. She still found no prejudice, because the extra discovery Younge proposed concerned facts within her own knowledge, was a "fishing expedition," or amounted to legal research. She declined to reach the policymaking-appointee exemption, finding that late assertion prejudicial, and recommended summary judgment on the personal-staff ground. The district court agreed, granting summary judgment even though it found sufficient evidence of discriminatory motive. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. It assumed without deciding that the exemption is an affirmative defense, noting that the Fourth and Fifth Circuits disagree on that point, and reaffirmed Hassan's rule that a court may consider an unpleaded affirmative defense at summary judgment if the plaintiff is not prejudiced. It found no prejudice, stressing that Younge never took up the magistrate judge's offer to reopen discovery and had conceded that the office's discovery responses referred to her as "personal staff" five times. In footnote 8 it rejected her argument that Rule 16 b 4's good-cause standard applied: "we simply treat unpleaded affirmative defenses differently from late motions to amend pleadings." On the merits, assuming the six-factor Laurie test governs, it held that there was no genuine dispute that she was Howard's personal staff.

item.title: 11/2/26 – Prep: Maxwell v. Dinis
item.description: Maxwell, a former lawyer, was convicted by a New Jersey federal jury in 2014 of RICO conspiracy, wire fraud and related counts arising from a scheme with members of La Cosa Nostra to take control of FirstPlus Financial Group, a Texas mortgage lender, and drain more than $14 million from it; he was sentenced in 2015 to 240 months plus three years of supervised release, the Third Circuit affirmed, United States versus Scarfo, from 2022, and he disputes the government's account of the conduct in a pending section 2255 motion. He has no disciplinary infractions, carries B O P's lowest recidivism-risk rating, and has worked as a cook and a law-library clerk, activities he says earn First Step Act time credits, which the Act says "shall be applied toward time in prerelease custody or supervised release", section 3632 d 4 C. After B O P denied his requests, beginning in 2020, for transfer to a halfway house or home confinement, he filed a pro se section 2241 petition in February 2022 alleging, among other things, that B O P was not counting some of his productive activities and owed him 42 to 48 months of credits. The magistrate judge and district court dismissed: the First Step Act claims were unexhausted because his grievances sought only CARES Act home confinement, and the CARES Act claim failed on the merits. The government defended the dismissal on exhaustion alone, but the Fifth Circuit affirmed on a ground neither side had raised: under the "bright-line rule" of Melot versus Bergami, a claim belongs in habeas only if success would automatically entitle the prisoner to accelerated release, so a request for a halfway house or home confinement must be brought as a civil-rights, Bivens, suit. It did not reach exhaustion, and in a footnote it set aside an unpublished contrary ruling on CARES Act home confinement, Cheek versus Warden, and described Maxwell's claim as arising under the First Step Act's elderly-offender pilot program, a description Maxwell disputed.

item.title: 10/14/26 – Prep: Salazar v. Paramount Global
item.description: In 2022 Michael Salazar signed up for a free email newsletter from 247Sports.com, a Paramount-owned college-sports site; he alleges that when he later watched videos on the site while logged into Facebook, the Meta Pixel embedded in the site sent Facebook his Facebook ID and the addresses of the video pages he viewed without his consent, and he seeks the VPPA's $2,500 in liquidated damages per class member plus punitive damages. The district court dismissed on the ground that he was not a "consumer" because the newsletter was not audiovisual, and a divided Sixth Circuit affirmed: Judge Nalbandian, joined by Judge Batchelder, read "goods or services from a video tape service provider" together with the statute's definition of a provider as one dealing in "prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials" and held that only audiovisual goods or services count, while Judge Bloomekatz dissented that the plain text limits the source of the goods or services, not their type. The circuits are split 2 to 2: the Second Circuit, in Salazar versus NBA, a parallel suit by the same plaintiff, and the Seventh Circuit read the definition to reach any of a provider's goods or services, including newsletters, while the D.C. Circuit sided with the Sixth in Pileggi versus Washington Newspaper Publishing Company, where a cert petition is pending. In opposing certiorari, Paramount argued the claim would fail anyway because 247Sports is not a "video tape service provider" and Pixel data is not "personally identifiable information," but the courts below assumed both points, the Sixth Circuit decided only the "consumer" question, and Paramount's merits brief does not press the alternative grounds. The Court denied the NBA's petition raising the same "consumer" question, along with a standing question, on December 8, 2025, and granted this one on January 26, 2026.

item.title: 10/13/26 – Prep: Beaird v. United States
item.description: In October 2022, Dallas police took a Glock pistol with an inserted 17-round magazine from Kendrick Beaird's waistband, the government says an officer saw him point it at another person; Beaird stresses that the gun was unloaded and the magazine was the factory standard, and he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a felon under section 922 g 1. Guideline section 2K2.1 a 3 raises the base offense level when the offense involved a semiautomatic firearm "capable of accepting a large capacity magazine," a phrase the guideline text does not define but Application Note 2 of the commentary defines as a magazine that could accept more than 15 rounds; applying the note raised Beaird's range from 51 to 63 to 63 to 78 months, and the district court imposed 72 months while stating it would have imposed the same sentence under any range. The Fifth Circuit summarily affirmed, treating the challenge as foreclosed by United States versus Vargas, en banc 2023, which held that Stinson survives Kisor versus Wilkie and that commentary controls even unambiguous guidelines, and by United States versus Martin, from 2024, which upheld this particular note. The circuits have divided over whether Kisor's limits apply to Guidelines commentary, though the government notes that every circuit to apply Kisor to the large-capacity-magazine note has upheld it. Neither party defends the judgment, Beaird argues for no deference at all, or, alternatively, Kisor's limits, and the United States argues that Stinson properly incorporates Kisor's limits and supports vacatur and remand while predicting the same sentence, so the Court appointed Anthony Dick to argue that Stinson remains correct as written.

item.title: 10/7/26 – Prep: Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guåhan
item.description: Since the 1980s the Air Force has disposed of expired and unexploded munitions by open burning and open detonation at Tarague Beach on Andersen Air Force Base in northern Guam, under a RCRA hazardous-waste permit administered by Guam EPA, which holds EPA-authorized permitting authority. In May 2021 the Air Force applied to renew the permit; Guam EPA issued a preliminary decision that October that neither granted nor denied it, and the application remains pending while operations continue under the expired permit. Prutehi Guåhan sued in January 2022, alleging the Air Force violated NEPA by failing to prepare an environmental impact statement before applying. The District of Guam dismissed for lack of final agency action, but a divided Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the application marked the consummation of the Air Force's decision to continue detonations and carried legal consequences under Bennett versus Spear, and that RCRA's permitting process does not displace NEPA; Judge VanDyke dissented that the application was a routine step in implementing an existing operation and that the majority's approach could reach almost any agency decision. The Court granted certiorari on March 9, 2026. Amici for the government include the Chamber of Commerce and 21 states led by West Virginia; amici for respondent include 11 states led by Washington, Guam and Pacific-territory community organizations, members of Congress, and the Virgin Islands Bar Association.

item.title: 6/4/26 – Decision: Sripetch v. Securities and Exchange Commission (9 to 0)
item.description: - Decided: June 4, 2026 - Vote: 9 to 0 - Majority: Gorsuch, for a unanimous Court - Concurrences: Thomas, alone. Argues that once Congress added section 78u d 7 in 2021 and separated "disgorgement" from "equitable remedies" in the limitations provisions, disgorgement became a legal remedy for which the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial; urges the Court to so hold in a future case and describes the SEC's practice of sending disgorged funds to the Treasury as a fines regime. - Dissents: None.

item.title: 10/6/26 – Prep: Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee
item.description: After the 2008 financial crisis, Intel's investment committee redesigned the plans' custom target-date funds and a diversified fund to allocate substantial shares, plaintiffs say roughly a third of some funds, to hedge funds, private equity, commodities, and other alternative assets, with the stated goal of dampening equity volatility. Participants sued in 2019, alleging the funds carried higher fees and chronically underperformed conventional target-date funds, peer-group averages, and market indices with heavier equity exposure, and that the fiduciaries breached ERISA's duties of prudence and loyalty. The district court dismissed for failure to plead a "meaningful benchmark," and the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that an underperformance claim must identify a comparator with similar aims, risks, and potential rewards, and that broad indices and ordinary target-date funds were not meaningful benchmarks for funds built to reduce equity risk. The Second, Seventh, Eighth, and Tenth Circuits apply versions of the same requirement; the Sixth Circuit declined to make a benchmark a pleading prerequisite in Johnson versus Parker-Hannifin Corporation, from 2024, and a cert petition in that case is pending. The Court granted certiorari on January 16, 2026, and the United States filed as amicus supporting Intel.

item.title: 10/5/26 – Prep: Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County
item.description: Boulder County and the City of Boulder sued Suncor and ExxonMobil in Colorado state court in 2018, pleading public and private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, civil conspiracy, and Colorado Consumer Protection Act claims, and seeking damages for local climate-adaptation costs, heat, drought, wildfire, reduced snowpack, they attribute to the companies' production and marketing of fossil fuels. After a removal fight that ended with the case back in state court, the trial court denied the companies' motion to dismiss on preemption grounds. In May 2025 the Colorado Supreme Court held that neither federal common law, the Clean Air Act, nor the federal foreign-affairs power bars the claims, reasoning that Boulder seeks compensation for the companies' conduct rather than regulation of anyone's emissions. The Court granted certiorari on February 23, 2026 and directed the parties to also address whether the interlocutory ruling is a reviewable final judgment under section 1257 and whether petitioners have Article Three standing. Roughly two dozen similar suits by states and municipalities are pending nationwide; the Trump administration filed an amicus brief supporting the companies, and more than 100 amicus briefs were filed in all.

item.title: 10/5/26 – Prep: Johnson v. United States Congress
item.description: Johnson received an 80 percent VA disability rating for service-connected PTSD. After he was convicted of state felonies and sentenced to 40 years, the VA reduced his compensation to the 10 percent rate under section 5313, which caps benefits for veterans incarcerated more than 60 days for a felony. Proceeding pro se, he sued Congress in the Middle District of Florida, alleging that section 5313 is a bill of attainder and denies equal protection; a magistrate judge recommended dismissal as frivolous and the district court agreed. The Eleventh Circuit vacated and ordered dismissal for want of jurisdiction, holding that section 511 a of the VJRA channels all claims touching veterans' benefits, including facial constitutional challenges to statutes, through the VA, the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, and the Federal Circuit. That ruling aligned the Eleventh Circuit with the Eighth and against the Second, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, and D.C. Circuits, which read Robison as preserving district-court jurisdiction over constitutional challenges to the statutes themselves. The government agreed that certiorari was warranted while defending the Eleventh Circuit on the merits; the Court granted on April 6, 2026. Eight amicus briefs support Johnson; none supports the government.
